PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA 
1325 G STREET, N.W., SUITE 800 
WASHINGTON, D.C. 20005

DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA, Order No. 23136 

I. 
INTRODUCTION 

1. 
By this Order,1 the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia 
(“Commission”) grants Verizon Washington, DC Inc.’s (“Verizon DC”) Request for District of 
Columbia Universal Service Trust Fund (“DC USTF”) Funding Application for the First Quarter 
of 20262 (“Request for the First Quarter of 2026”) for the provision of wireline Lifeline telephone 
service to low-income District of Columbia customers. The Commission directs the DC USTF 
Administrator to reimburse Verizon DC the $7,250.16 requested by Verizon DC for the First 
Quarter of 2026 within fifteen (15) days of the date of this Order. 

II. 
BACKGROUND 

2. 
On July 16, 2026, Verizon DC filed its Request for the Fourth Quarter of 2026, 
seeking reimbursement of $7,250.16 for the provision of Lifeline service to a total of 528 
qualifying low-income customers3 from January through March 2026. In its Request, Verizon DC 
submits the data and methodology used to calculate the reimbursement amount as well as the 
confidential client lists of its Lifeline customers.4 Verizon DC also includes information on the 
Economy II Lifeline applications processed by Verizon DC during the First Quarter of 2026.5

authority to act and issue orders on the following matters: . . . s. Unopposed Requests for Universal Service Trust Fund 
Reimbursement filed by Verizon Washington DC, Inc.”). Any party may file a petition for reconsideration of the 
General Counsel’s decision with the Commission.

of 2026”), filed July 16, 2026.

actual Lifeline customer count was lower than 528 for the First Quarter of 2026 (there were 180 customers in January 
2026, 174 customers in February 2026, and 174 customers in March 2026).

Verizon DC requests that Solix, Inc. (“Solix”), the DC USTF Administrator, confirm that the

3. 
Solix filed its Recommendation on July 22, 2026.7 Solix recommends 
reimbursement of $7,250.16 because it can validate the eligibility of all Verizon DC Lifeline 
customers. Solix bases this recommendation on its review of the customer data presented by 
Verizon DC in the Request for the First Quarter of 2026, and a comparison of this data to the 
customer data in the National Lifeline Accountability Database (“NLAD”) operated by the 
Universal Service Administrative Company (“USAC”). Solix represents that its analysis showed 
that NLAD’s list matched the list provided by Verizon DC. Solix recommends reimbursement for 
the entire amount requested by Verizon DC in its Request for the First Quarter of 2026.8 

III. 
DISCUSSION 

4. 
In Order No. 15303,9 the Commission established the standard for ruling on DC 
USTF reimbursement requests. In that Order, the Commission reviewed a prior version of Title 15 
of the District of Columbia Municipal Regulations (“DCMR”) § 2803.2, and determined that the 
language permits reimbursement for “each eligible customer.”10 Since the District Department of 
Energy and Environment (“DOEE”) verified customer eligibility at that time, the Commission 
reasoned that only those customers on DOEE’s customer lists would be eligible for reimbursement 
by the DC USTF.11 Although the Lifeline Eligibility Verification Administrator changed from 
DOEE to Solix, and now, as of May 7, 2019, to USAC,12 it does not change the requirement that 
an eligible telecommunications carrier may only be reimbursed for those customers previously 
determined to be eligible for Lifeline service.13

national transition plan mandated by the Federal Communications Commission (“FCC”). See In the Matter of Lifeline

Connect America Fund, WC Docket Nos. 11-42, 09-197, 10-90, Third Report and Order, Further Report and Order 
and Order on Reconsideration, rel. April 27, 2016. After May 7, 2019, USAC is now responsible for determining the 
eligibility of Lifeline applicants in the District of Columbia and for maintaining the customer information for Lifeline 
service customers in NLAD. 

13 
The Commission notes that the FCC is working to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse through the Lifeline and 
Link Up Reform and Modernization; Lifeline and Link Up; Federal-State Joint Board on Universal Service; 
Advancing Broadband Availability Through Digital Literacy Training, WC Docket Nos. 11-42, 03-109, 12-23, and

be reimbursed $7,250.16 for the First Quarter of 2026. Solix shall pay Verizon DC this amount 
within 15 days of the date of this Order. 

THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED THAT: 

6. 
Verizon Washington, DC Inc.’s Request for DC Universal Service Trust Fund 
Funding Application for the First Quarter of 2026 is GRANTED; and 

7. 
The District of Columbia Universal Service Trust Fund Administrator shall 
reimburse Verizon Washington, DC Inc. the $7,250.16 requested by Verizon Washington, DC Inc.

PARTIAL CONCURRENCE 
OF COMMISSIONER BEVERLY TO ORDER NO. 23133 
1. 
Although I concur that this effort to establish an IDSP framework is a significant 
step forward, I think we need a bigger step. In response to my independent Notice of Inquiry on 
this subject, DOEE submitted an order from the New York Public Service Commission that gives 
a useful rule-based approach to IDSP rather than a framework composed of loose guidelines that 
basically leaves all the plan details to Pepco’s discretion. DOEE also suggested that, where 
appropriate, we align our plan with efforts already underway in the Maryland Public Service 
Commission. I agree with both suggestions. 

2. 
There are a few deficiencies in this plan that warrant comment. First, the draft 
framework does not provide evaluation criteria, including compliance with the District’s RPS 
(including the solar carve-out), or a Commission approval process. 

3. 
Second, the ability of the Commission to implement an effective IDSP requires a 
fulsome dataset, which may require an expansion of data collection and reporting by the Company. 
The draft framework appears to limit decision-making on data access to the Company, and to 
already-existing datasets. In my view, an IDSP should require, at a minimum: overhead/unground 
wires by voltage; number and capacity of substations; number and capacity of transformers; 
monitoring and measurement capabilities (i.e. SCADA); annual/seasonal peak demand by 
substation zone and feeder; line losses; number, capabilities, and locations of islandable 
microgrids; and historical demand-side management investments and resulting peak demand 
reduction. While the draft framework does include reporting of “Historical O&M and Capital 
Spending by project and by Executive Categories, for a minimum of five years of historic data,” 
the reasoning behind the expenditures should also be required. The draft framework calls for the 
number and type of DER, but should also include the capacity of the DER and location by 
substation zone/feeder. While the draft framework calls for baseline information on EV chargers, 
it does not specify the inclusion of their capacity or location information. The IDSP should also 
include detailed requirements for how the Company reports planned retirements. 

4. 
Third, the draft framework does not address whether forecasts will be provided in 

Partial Concurrence to Order No. 23133 

Page 2 

both MWh and MW, whether coincident/non-coincident peaks should be reported, or the provision 
of probabilistic DER forecasting. The draft framework provides for hourly DER forecasts at the 
substation and feeder level, but includes language to allow the Company to avoid compliance. The 
draft framework does not require the Company to model compliance with the solar carve-out of 
the RPS. In my view, the DER, load, and net forecasts should have specific outputs that include 
both hourly and peak demand forecasts at the substation zone and feeder. The information should 
be mandatory. Otherwise, it is not possible to assess DER as grid resources, which is the purpose 
of an integrated planning exercise. Stakeholders should have a chance to weigh in on DER, load, 
and net forecasting before an IDSP is implemented. Modeling scenarios should address RPS 
compliance. 

5. 
Fourth, the draft framework provides room for the Company to include and also 
improve its hosting capacity analysis (“HCA”), but leaves these improvements as optional. The 
Company’s HCA needs to be reformed to align with national best practices. Maintaining the overly 
conservative HCA may result in the Company over-estimating grid needs under various DER 
forecasts. An amended HCA methodology should be Commission-approved and provide for 
annual data validation. 

6. 
Fifth, the draft framework does not require Pepco to provide its methodology and 
calculations for SAIDI, SAIFI, CAIDI, and CEMI-3 for evaluation by stakeholders and the 
Commission. I believe this should be expressly required. The draft framework requires the 
provision of data regarding grid needs/constraints, but does not specify the required data. A grid 
needs assessment should be data-driven, and each identified grid need should include a description 
of the deficiency, associated engineering characteristics, and timing of the need. 

7. 
Sixth, that brings me to the prioritization of grid needs. The draft framework “Cost-
Effectiveness and Equity” section addresses a cost-effectiveness prioritization once solutions have 
already been identified, but the draft framework does not address prioritization of grid needs 
themselves. The grid needs assessment should be driven by a prioritization exercise, including 
criteria, methodology, and outputs from a ranking exercise of grid needs resulting in a transparent 
explanation and categorization of the needs that require immediate action, near-term action, or 
longer-term action. 

8. 
Seventh, the draft framework addresses the inclusion non-wires alternatives 
(“NWA”) but does not state whether NWA, DER, demand-side management, and rate design are 
reviewed on equal footing with traditional solutions. While the draft framework incorporates the 
eventual Commission-approved BCA framework in a cost-effectiveness section, it does not require 
the Company to use the BCA as part of the evaluation criteria for solution selection, instead leaving 
evaluation criteria up to the Company. While there is an option to provide cost data based on 
solicitations, there is no requirement for the Company to engage in solicitations to determine the 
capability, availability, and detailed costs for NWA. The IDSP needs to explicitly review all NWA

on equal footing with traditional solutions, and require the provision of capabilities and detailed 
cost information of options. Selections should be explicitly based on the Commission-approved 
BCA framework, and any other evaluation criteria determined by the working group. 

9. 
Finally, the draft framework does not address the development of an Action Plan 
for Commission approval. An Action Plan submitted for Commission approval should include the 
following: plans encouraging the deployment of DERs, including contracting through NWAs; 
plans for permitting, constructing, preparing required reports and other significant activities where 
replacement, upgrades, or expansion of utility infrastructure has been identified as the best option; 
plans for the retirement or retrofit of existing major equipment; a timeline that establishes the 
sequence of events for each action; and plans to solicit competitive bids.

The Commission appreciates the work undertaken by the Stakeholders to consider

continue the existing regulatory asset or establish a new regulatory asset to record the incremental

Pepco base rate case.

deciding whether the Rider SCADRRC should continue beyond the two-year pilot, the 
Commission directs Pepco to: (1) conduct market research and additional analysis; (2) convene

16.

support a final determination regarding the Program’s structure, funding, or permanent 
continuation. AARP DC and NCLC support continued assistance, while DOEE and OPC support 
an extended pilot. DOEE’s analysis provides suggestive evidence that the Program reaches 
communities likely in need of assistance. At the same time, Pepco and DOEE identify important 
data limitations, OPC calls for a broader fairness and impact analysis, and AOBA raises concerns 
regarding demonstrated need, cost shifting, and cumulative rate impacts. These competing 
considerations favor continuation of a defined pilot with a cost cap, and an opportunity to collect 
additional data related to the program’s benefits and consumer impacts. This two-year pilot 
extension preserves continuity for current participants while permitting the Commission to obtain 
information that the technical conference record does not presently contain.

sufficient time to develop and approve an evaluation plan, conduct market research, collect 
additional Program data, present resulting information to Stakeholders, and develop a final 
recommendation before the pilot expires.

I. 
INTRODUCTION 

1. 
By this Order,1 the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia 
(“Commission”) authorizes and directs the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco”) to release

(“MEDSIS”) Pilot Project Fund Subaccount (“MEDSIS Fund Subaccount”) to Ecogy Energy 
(“Ecogy”) within fifteen (15) days from the date of this Order. 

II. 
BACKGROUND 

2. 
As a condition of the PHI-Exelon Merger, a MEDSIS Pilot Project Fund of $21.55 
million was created to fund grid modernization projects to benefit District ratepayers.2 In Order 
No. 20286, the Commission established the Pilot Projects Governance Board (“Board”) to 
recommend pilot projects and develop Requests for Proposals (“RFPs”), which would be 
submitted to the Commission for issuance. Responses to the RFPs would be reviewed and ranked 
by the Commission, which would then select an offeror and award a contract for the pilot project 
utilizing pilot project funds.3

INTRODUCTION

electricity supplier in the District of Columbia (“District”) in Order No. 16446.2 On June 5, 2026, 
Viridian filed an Application with the Commission to surrender its electricity supplier license.3

III.
DISCUSSION
3.
According to 15 DCMR § 4602.10 (a)(1), a licensed electricity supplier wishing to
cease providing services in the District is required to provide written notice to the Commission of 
the licensee’s intention to cease providing electricity service to its customers and inform its 
customers of the choice to revert to the default service provider or another electricity supplier. 
Section 4602.10 (a)(2) also requires that the surrendering licensee provide to the Commission an 
example or copy of the notice it provided to its customers and, upon the Commission’s receipt of 
such notice, may order the licensee to provide such further notice to its customers or the public as 
the Commission deems necessary, and/or take such other action that the Commission considers 
appropriate.6 
4.
In the instant case, Viridian’s Application provides the required notice to the
Commission of its intention to surrender its electricity supplier license.7 Viridian also states that 
the notice requirement to customers is not applicable because it has no customers in the District.8 
Accordingly, Viridian’s Application satisfies the notice requirement with regard to the cessation 
of service. 
5.
In all other respects, Viridian’s Application conforms with Commission
requirements for a surrendering licensee. Commission records confirm the Applicant’s submission 
of the case number, order number, and date the Applicant’s license was granted.9 Viridian avers, 
and Commission records confirm that the Applicant’s most recent survey response indicates no 
jurisdictional revenue and that it owes no outstanding debt or fees.10 In addition, the Applicant 
states that it has no outstanding consumer complaints.11 Lastly, the signed Application from an 
officer of Viridian attests to the truth and accuracy of the information submitted.12 
6.
Based upon the preceding information, the Commission grants Viridian’s request
to surrender its electricity supplier license granted by Order No. 16446. Cancellation of Viridian’s 
electricity supplier license shall become effective upon the issuance of this Order. Should Viridian 
seek to re-enter the District’s electricity market in the future, it shall have to reapply for an 
electricity supplier license pursuant to Chapter 46 of the Commission’s rules.

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
1. 
By this Order,1 the Public Service Commission of the District of Columbia 
(“Commission”) directs the Potomac Electric Power Company (“Pepco” or “Company”) 
to deposit $25,000 via ACH/wire transfer, into the Treasury of the District of Columbia, as 
shown in Attachment A of this Order, by July 30, 2026. The funds are needed by the Office 
of the People’s Counsel for the District of Columbia (“OPC” or “Office”) to meet expenses 
incurred by OPC in carrying out its statutory mandate to represent ratepayers in Formal 
Case No. 1182. 
II. 
BACKGROUND 

2. 
On July 9, 2026, OPC filed a Notice of Agency Fund Requirements 
(“NOAFR” or “Notice”) in Formal Case No. 1182 notifying the Commission of the need 
for an Order directing Pepco to deposit $25,000 into the Treasury of the District of 
Columbia, to the credit of the fiduciary account known as the “Office of the People’s 
Counsel Agency Fund”, to meet expenses incurred by OPC in carrying out its statutory 
mandate to represent ratepayers in this proceeding.2 In its NOAFR, OPC seeks to retain 
the technical consulting services of GDS Associates, Inc. to, among other things, provide 
technical assistance to OPC regarding electric utility distribution system planning and 
integrated distribution system planning.3 OPC’s filing indicates that the Office delivered 
a copy of the proposed Notice and a proposed Commission order to the Pepco attorney

III. 
DISCUSSION 
3. 
The Commission has reviewed the information submitted by OPC in 
support of this Notice and finds that the Office has provided all of the relevant information 
in its filing pursuant to 15 DCMR § 1405.2. Formal Case No. 1182 is a non-rate case 
proceeding or other investigation. The Commission’s most recent determination of the 
Company’s District of Columbia jurisdictional valuation is $3,302,900,00 million.6 
Calculation of this jurisdictional valuation against the “one-twentieth of one percent” 
limitations set out in D.C. Code § 34-912(a)(3) yields a maximum individual non-rate case 
assessment of $1,651,450. Thus far in calendar year 2026, OPC has assessed Pepco 
$145,473 for non-rate case proceedings or other investigations. Accordingly, OPC’s 
Agency Fund Requirements of $25,000 will not cause the Office to exceed its statutory 
millage limit. The Commission finds that this Notice is consistent with the statutory 
authority and rules issued by the Office; is supported by findings, which are sustained by 
substantial evidence in the record submitted with the Notice; and is within the limitations 
enumerated in D.C. Code § 34-912(a)(3).
